sentence: The NHS says that anyone who has had three or more miscarriages should talk to a GP.

The options are waiting for the pregnancy to pass on its own, medical management with tablets, or surgery to remove the pregnancy from the womb.
NICE says clinicians should discuss all the options so that the person can make an informed choice.
NICE gives expectant management, which means waiting, as the first-line approach for a confirmed miscarriage.
Where it is clinically appropriate, NICE says surgery can be chosen, and it is done in a theatre under general anaesthetic.
NICE's 2026 update recommends mifepristone together with misoprostol for the medical management of missed miscarriage.
The NHS home recovery advice includes resting as needed and using paracetamol for pain.
The NHS says sex is best avoided until symptoms have gone because of a risk of infection.
The NHS says that having a miscarriage can be difficult both physically and emotionally, and that for some people it takes longer to recover emotionally.
It says the GP surgery or pregnancy unit can give information about counselling and other support services, and that support is also available for partners.

The Miscarriage Association lists NHS routes to support including the GP, the early pregnancy unit, a bereavement midwife or nurse, perinatal mental health services and NHS Talking Therapies, where self-referral is available.
